name: O(n²), except when it's O(n)
hook: Insertion sort is O(n²). Except when it's O(n). Its real cost is how out of order your data is.
hook_slide: Insertion sort is O(n²). *Except when it's O(n).*
hook_sub: Its real cost is how out of order your data is.
caption: Insertion sort takes the next element, shifts the larger ones right, and drops it into place.
Reverse-sorted input is the worst case: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] takes 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = {small_shifts} shifts, and {n} reversed elements take {reversed_shifts}.
Already sorted? {sorted_shifts} shifts and {sorted_cmp} comparisons, one per element. With {pairs} neighbouring pairs swapped: {nearly_shifts} shifts.

Every shift fixes exactly one inversion (a pair that's out of order), so the work is O(n + I), where I is the number of inversions. That's why it survives in practice: real data is often almost sorted.
Where have you seen insertion sort hiding inside a faster sort? 👇
cta: Then merge sort, and the proof that no comparison sort beats O(n log n).

p: Take the next element, shift larger elements right, and drop it into its place.
Reverse-sorted input: each insertion shifts all the way back. The triangular sum, O(n²).
An inversion is a pair that is out of order relative to each other. Every shift resolves exactly one.
So the total work is O(n + I), where I is the inversion count: how far the input is from sorted, not n outright.
